summary:
BoysFire is a fire record for Peru that integrates heat-spot data from NASA’s MODIS and VIIRS satellites into a single, comparable time series dating back to the year 2000.

This integration was necessary because, if counted at face value, the number of heat spots appears to have increased 7.9-fold since 2012—a rise that did not actually occur; rather, satellite technology simply improved. Through our harmonization process, this ratio is adjusted to 0.95.

Based on this data series, the system provides:

A calendar and map: a day-by-day view spanning 26 years, compared against historical norms for each date, down to the district level.
Prevention: a risk index (ranging from 0 to 11) for the next 7 days—calculated using real-time weather data—accompanied by actionable recommendations.
Citizen reporting: users can report smoke or fire, with each report cross-referenced against satellite data.
Alerts: notifications are sent to local contacts in the affected area, with a system in place to track their response.

The problem

Peru has more than 25 years of satellite fire data, but it is hard to compare across time. MODIS (1 km, since 2000) and VIIRS (375 m, since 2012) see fires differently. Simply counting hotspots makes it look like fires multiplied by 7.9× after 2012. That increase never happened: the satellite just got better. Communities and authorities are left without a trustworthy answer to "is this season normal, or critical?"

What it does

Harmonized record (2000–2026): one comparable series of fire activity from 2.1 million NASA FIRMS detections, down to Peru's 25 departments, 195 provinces and 1,826 districts. After harmonization the false 7.9× jump drops to 0.95×.

Fire calendar: every day of 27 years colored against what is normal for that date: normal, above normal, or critical.

Interactive map and timeline: regions or individual hotspots, six basemaps (including NASA GIBS imagery), and a play mode that replays fire day by day.

Prevention: a 0–11 fire-risk score for the next 7 days, built from six factors (strong wind, dry vegetation, dry air, heat, fire season, active fire), each explained in plain language with recommended actions.

Community reports: anyone can report smoke or fire from a phone. The report is placed in its district and compared with the nearest satellite hotspot, so operators can tell whether the satellite backs it up.

Alert coordination: alerts for high risk, active fires and community reports, routed to local contacts for the affected area, with a tracked status (open, notified, verifying, confirmed, dismissed) and a logged response history.

Monitoring panel: 11 automatic health checks every 15 minutes on data freshness, weather and operations.

How we built it

Method: hotspots are mapped onto an H3 grid and counted as active cell-days rather than raw detections. A two-part calibration against the VIIRS S-NPP reference removes the sensor change, and a ±7-day climatology with a 90th-percentile threshold defines "critical".

Validation: on held-out years, monthly correlation is 0.995 and daily correlation 0.82, with the 99th percentile off by only +1%.

Stack: Python (data processing), SQL Server 2022, Spring Boot (Java 25), Angular with Tailwind CSS, MapLibre GL and ECharts, packaged with Docker and served over HTTPS from a cloud VM.

Data and sources

NASA FIRMS: MODIS (Terra, Aqua) and VIIRS (S-NPP, NOAA-20) active fire detections, archive and near-real-time.

NASA GIBS: dated satellite imagery basemap.

Open-Meteo: weather for the risk forecast (not a NASA source).

Honest limitations

A hotspot is a possible fire, not a confirmed one. Confirmation comes from local contacts and operators.

Before 2012, about three quarters of the yearly index is estimated background; the app draws those values hatched, never as solid.

The risk score flags favorable conditions for fire; it does not predict individual fires.

The hosted demo shows satellite data up to November 15, 2026. The near-real-time ingestion pipeline is built, but is not running in the demo.

Alert delivery to Telegram is implemented; without a bot token the demo records deliveries as simulated.
